narrative:
The model predicted a 60.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score was the single strongest influence, and it worked in your favor. At 46, it sits well above the average of 37 among students who were admitted, pushing the model noticeably toward predicting that you would pass the bar.

Unfortunately, two academic performance measures pulled the prediction in the opposite direction and ultimately outweighed the positive LSAT signal. Your first-year and third-year class rankings both placed you in the third decile of your school. These rankings are substantially below the averages of roughly sixth and fifth deciles seen among accepted students. The model interpreted these lower relative standings as strong indicators that you would struggle with the bar exam, and they became the dominant reasons for the rejection.

In short, although your LSAT performance was excellent, the model gave greater weight to your class-rank history and concluded you were more likely than not to fail the bar on the first try.

What you should do next is straightforward: retake key courses or seek additional academic support to raise your class standing, then reapply. Stronger decile rankings would likely flip the prediction in your favor while keeping your solid LSAT advantage.
